main.title: Creator visibility
context: Problem: Over 14,000 partner creators in the Ubisoft Creator Program felt ignored because the brand rarely gave feedback on their work, while internal teams lacked a structured process to share partner content.
Outcome: I designed and pitched a multi-department workflow to regularly feature creator content on official channels, securing approval from key department leads to begin trial rollouts.

sections.title: Human Friction
description: In the Ubisoft Creator Program, over 14,000 partner creators felt invisible. They put a lot of effort into their content, but a lack of feedback from the brand hurt their trust and loyalty.

sections.title: Business Opportunity
description: At the same time, Ubisoft was missing out. The company was leaving a lot of organic visibility and Earned Media Value (EMV) on the table because internal teams lacked a structured approach. As the main UX designer under the guidance of my Design Manager, my goal was to build a realistic workflow that bridged this dual gap within strict enterprise constraints.

sections.title: Discovery
description: To validate creator friction, I started by looking at 12 other entertainment brands, including EA, Riot, and LEGO, to see how they handled creator visibility. This revealed that while huge influencers got plenty of PR attention, nobody had a visible structured way to highlight smaller micro and nano-creators.

Concurrently, I looked at over 20 partner channels and read through more than 60 Discord community reports. The research confirmed the core issue: creators felt they were working in a vacuum because there was no internal system to discover or give feedback on their work.

sections.title: Ideation Workshop
description: The root of the problem was internal confusion, so I focused on internal teams instead of asking the creators to fix our handoff issues.

I co-structured and facilitated a two-hour workshop with six internal leads. We used an Impact/Effort matrix to evaluate 24 different ideas and converged on official channel reposting as the most realistic solution. This session also served to identify which key departments needed to be integrated into the pipeline.

sections.title: Mapping the Process
description: Following the workshop, I conducted interviews with stakeholders integrated during that session to refine the pipeline around their real-world constraints and needs.

This research revealed how complex the organization really was: six different departments had to coordinate across a mix of publishing tools, task trackers, and community platforms. Over five iterations, I mapped out a workflow that separated global asset approvals from local market publishing, while making sure we still hit mandatory brand safety checks.

sections.title: Large-Scale Validation
description: Once the internal workflow was established, I designed a survey for Ubisoft's Discord community of over 2,000 creators to make sure this approach actually matched what they wanted.

sections.title: RACI Governance
description: Following a recommendation from my Design Manager, I built a RACI framework to turn this workflow into something teams could actually use. I defined two distinct scenarios: a proactive model for planned campaign activations and a reactive model for spontaneous community clips.

sections.title: Persuasive Storytelling
description: To secure executive buy-in, I translated these models into visual storyboards. By showing the exact journey of a clip (from a creator posting it on Discord, through brand safety checks, and finally onto a local social media channel), I turned a technical handoff into a story that was easy to follow.
This approach helped me get approval from three key department leads, giving us a blueprint ready for testing.

sections.title: Impact and Reflections
description: This project taught me that a great solution is not just usable, but must also be actively adopted by its users. Trying to book time with busy internal staff forced me to create really tight, efficient interview guides.
I also learned that visual storytelling is a powerful way to explain technical processes to business leaders, turning a heavy operational proposal into something they actually want to support.

main.title: VMT
main.description: improving the usability of an industrial simulator
context: Problem: Airbus Helicopters created a 3D simulator to train technicians on complex maintenance tasks, but instructors were underusing it in class. Navigating the software was cumbersome enough that trainers often preferred relying on physical mockups, missing out on the digital tool's flexibility.

Outcome: I mapped out 28 core usability friction points and presented six key interaction recommendations, including a dual-mode camera and a radial contextual menu. Engineering leads at Airbus Helicopters and Telespazio validated and approved the overall specification package.

sections.title: Context
description: Airbus Helicopters built the Virtual Maintenance Trainer (VMT) to help technicians practice helicopter maintenance across over fifty simulated failure scenarios. On paper, it offered a flexible way to scale training without needing constant access to expensive physical mockups, but it struggled to gain regular traction in actual classrooms.

sections.title: The Challenge
description: The primary goal was to fix low adoption rates. Instructors frequently set the simulator aside during live lessons in favor of paper manuals or physical aircraft mockups. My mission was to uncover why trainers avoided the software and provide practical recommendations to improve its intuitiveness and learning efficiency.

Working as a UX Consultant intern through the IMS Laboratory, my goal was to pinpoint the ergonomic friction points behind this low adoption and redesign the software interactions around real classroom teaching habits.

sections.title: Discovery
description: To understand how the simulator operated, I did an initial walkthrough to catch obvious technical friction, such as navigation dead ends. I also reviewed three doctoral theses on aeronautical simulation learning to build a semi-structured interview grid tailored to the Airbus training environment.

sections.title: Qualitative Research
description: During this early phase, a key insight emerged: B2 Avionics instructors adapted to the same type of software easily, but B1.3 Mechanical instructors rejected it because the digital space offered no physical feedback for engine parts. To dig deeper, I went to Aérocampus Aquitaine and interviewed five instructors and two trainees about their frustrations, processing the transcriptions with WhisperAI.

sections.title: Field Observations
description: When observing live classes, I saw that instructors barely touched the simulator, defaulting immediately to physical mockups. I adapted my approach and started holding informal contextual discussions with them between training sessions. They explained that setting up and navigating around the 3D space took too much effort, breaking the natural pacing of their lessons.

sections.title: Quantitative Data
description: To support these conversations with hard data, I sent a survey to active instructors. I got 11 responses and combined them with an older internal Airbus study of 18 users. Looking at this group of 29 participants, the numbers confirmed a widespread trend: 70% used the software less than once a month, and 55% cited 3D camera movement and interface clarity as main obstacles.

sections.title: Heuristic Synthesis
description: To structure these findings objectively, I categorized the interview and survey data using a 10-point ergonomic heuristic framework. This allowed me to systematically evaluate factors such as cognitive load and ergonomic transparency.

sections.title: Key Issues
description: I mapped out 28 distinct usability issues and proposed 25 concrete recommendations to fix them. To keep this case study focused, I have isolated the three biggest friction points:

• unstandardized camera navigation disoriented users during engine inspections.
• nested menus constantly forced instructors to look away from the task while lecturing.
• selecting small 3D engine components required exact mouse accuracy with zero visual hover affordance.

sections.title: Interaction Specification
description: Because my mission focused on interaction architecture rather than visual assets, I created interaction guidelines to solve those specific problems.
I proposed a dual-mode camera system combining standard WASD movement for navigating rooms with automatic orbit controls centered on selected components.
To reduce menu dependency, I designed a cursor-anchored radial menu using Fitts's Law to give instant access to common actions.
Finally, I specified permissive click tolerances, component outlining, and structured error messages to eliminate guesswork.

sections.title: Outcomes and Takeaways
description: The final deliverables included a 63-page comprehensive UX analysis report detailing all 28 usability blockers and 25 technical specifications. Knowing that long reports rarely get read in full, I also put together a presentation highlighting the six most impactful strategic ideas.
The engineering leads at Airbus Helicopters and Telespazio agreed with the findings and formally approved the recommendations.

Looking back, stepping away from formal observations and just talking to instructors in their environment was the right call. It showed me that no matter how detailed a technical simulation is, it won't work if the interaction design ignores human cognitive limits.

main.title: Emco
context: Problem: Evaluating workplace well-being usually relies on subjective surveys. We needed to create a mobile app that could take raw, objective biometric data and turn it into clear insights about a worker's cognitive load and stress.

Outcome: During a five-day academic sprint, I designed a 20-screen prototype that visually separated sudden emotional stress from general cognitive fatigue. By swapping a confusing heatmap for a simple 2D grid with a timeline slider, we made the data much easier for ergonomists to read.

sections.title: Context
sections.description: Corporate ergonomists look at workplace well-being, but they usually have to rely on subjective, after-the-fact surveys.The EmCo project was about building an objective tool to turn raw biometric data into clear Quality of Work Life indicators.

sections.title: The Challenge
description: Emotion and mental workload cause similar physical reactions, but they happen on different temporal scales. Emotions are quick spikes, while cognitive load represents sustained resource mobilization. The main UX challenge was finding a way to show these two different realities visually without overwhelming the user with raw data.
Working with a team of six, my job was to figure out the information architecture and design the UI, putting together a 20-screen mobile prototype.

sections.title: Making Sense of the Data
sections.description: Raw data is hard to read on the fly. To keep things clear, I turned complex biometric streams into human-readable status labels like 'Productive Focus' or 'Critical Overload.'

sections.title: Privacy
sections.description: To handle patient privacy during live sessions, I added a FaceID-style unlock. This let ergonomists quickly check who they were monitoring without the long-term interaction friction of passwords.

sections.title: Rapid Execution
sections.description: Because we only had five days from start to finish, I kept the UI design phase to just two days. To save time, I used AI tools to get quick feedback on my wireframes before we ran usability tests with five cognitive engineering professors and PhD researchers acting as proxy users on day three.

sections.title: Usability Evaluation
sections.description: Our testing showed that people liked the concept (+1.5 Stimulation), but it also pointed out a major usability flaw (-0.5 Pragmatic Quality). We had originally used heatmaps to show emotion, and they were simply too dense and confusing to read during a longer monitoring session.

sections.title: Empirical Iteration
description: To fix this, I made a few key changes to filter visual noise and gain affordance:

• I dropped the complex heatmaps in favor of a simple 2-dimensional grid based on Russell's model. By plotting discrete subject markers, the eye is instantly guided to critical outliers rather than scanning a chaotic 3D map.
• I paired this grid with a temporal slider, letting users track short emotional peaks and separate them from long-term fatigue.
• I added explicit threshold baselines across all the charts to remove interpretive guesswork, and moved extra actions into a simple menu to keep the main screen focused on the data.

sections.title: Takeaways
description: Building this prototype in a week meant we had to focus only on the most important features. Testing taught us a hard lesson about overcomplicating data visualization: simple is almost always better.
If we were to take this further, the next step would be testing the updated design in the field with actual corporate ergonomists to see how it holds up in a real workplace.

main.shortDescription: decoupling emotional state from cognitive workload

projects.title: Stealth startup
projects.shortDescription: design system of a social discovery app
context: Problem: The founders initially wanted a UI refresh for their social discovery app that had a completely new matching mechanic. But before building it, we needed to prove users actually wanted an alternative to swiping.
Outcome: A survey of over 300 people showed that 77.5% were tired of swiping. Based on this, I designed the app's core flows and a full design system to hand off over 100 screens to developers.

sections.title: Validating the Strategy
description: The founders originally hired me for a basic UI refresh, but they also wanted to introduce an innovative new matching mechanic. I suggested we dig into the UX first to validate if people actually wanted this. We ran a survey with over 300 users, and the data backed up their hypothesis: 77.5% of people were completely burned out and rejected traditional swipe interfaces.

sections.title: Core Mechanics
description: To make this new vision work, I designed an interaction hub restricted to a specific evening window (18h - 22h). This helped gather users online at the same time and reduced choice fatigue. To balance out the limited hours, I also mapped out a straightforward monetization flow with premium subscriptions and micro-transactions for immediate account refills.

sections.title: Interaction Design
description: The main product loop relies on an innovative, fast-paced mechanic, so the UI needed to be focused to keep cognitive load low. I set up a mutual 'Spark' decision gate to filter who gets access to direct messaging.

sections.title: Safety
description: Knowing 56% of female users face harassment, I also designed a quick, always-accessible reporting flow. This lets users block and report abusers instantly without getting lost in the navigation menus.

sections.title: Design System
description: To support the technical requirements behind the new mechanic and messaging, I built a Figma design system. By using 69 variables, it easily managed the brand's dark-mode theme and neon accents. This setup made handing the designs over to developers much faster, covering 7 interactive flows and over 100 high-fidelity screens.

sections.title: Final Deliverables
description: The final deliverables included custom iconography, clear microcopy using the PACE method to minimize friction, and a pitch deck for investors. This deck helped clearly present our UX strategy as a real alternative in the market.

projects.title: UCD sprint
context: Problem: We needed to rapidly adapt to three different industries (bike security, smart desks, and retail carts) to research, design and test UX concepts within tight academic deadlines.
Outcome: We designed an automated bike lock, built a mobile prototype for a smart desk, and ran a field test that proved a digital shopping cart app wasn't actually useful for real shoppers.

sections.title: Sprint Context
description: Following the Double Diamond framework, this project sprint simulated fast-paced agency conditions across three separate product domains. The goal was to adapt to unfamiliar industries, build design systems, and run real-world field tests.

sections.title: Phase 1: Conceptual Architecture (Ridar, Urban Mobility Security)
Field Observations
description: Bike theft results in 400,000 stolen bikes annually in France. To figure out why, we conducted observations and interviews at transit hubs in Bordeaux (Sainte-Catherine Street and Bergonié).

sections.title: Research Insights
description: Our research identified micro-stops as a critical vulnerability. Based on this, we mapped out three personas (the delivery driver, the rushed parent, and the determined ecologist). Since it takes an average of 23.2 seconds to secure a U-lock, people making fast stops often skip locking their bikes entirely just to save time

sections.title: Ideation
description: To eliminate obvious concepts, our team ran a 15-minute ideation purge, leaving a dozen viable ideas. We evaluated these on a matrix structured along two axes (Standalone Hardware vs. Bike-Integrated, and Passive Security vs. Smart Monitoring).

sections.title: Prioritization
description: Scoring the surviving concepts on effectiveness, feasibility, and originality led us to Ridar: a phygital security device integrated directly inside the seat post. It auto-arms as the cyclist walks away, eliminating that 23.2-second friction.

sections.title: Visual Storyboarding
description: To explain the concept, I illustrated a storyboard centered on a delivery driver persona. It shows how Ridar protects his bike without needing manual interaction during quick pick-ups. The system just works in the background and sends an alert to his phone if someone tries to move the bike.

sections.title: Phase 2: Systems Design (DeskFriend, Remote Workspace Ergonomics)
Rescoping the Brief
description: Transitioning to workspace ergonomics, our team inherited a heavy student spec sheet for a smart desk controller that presented 11 fragmented themes (some packing up to three sub-features each). Instead of building a cluttered interface, we ran a workshop to narrow the scope down to four main UX pillars.

sections.title: Rapid Architecture
description: To align the team, we sketched out our ideas on a whiteboard, turning those pillars into a simple control interface with six modular UI cards.

sections.title: Prototyping
description: Stepping in as Visual Design Lead, I built the Figma prototype from scratch using Auto layout rules and reusable component libraries. The main feature was a Focus Mode that blocks out notifications and lets you use your phone as a tactile desk remote.

sections.title: Phase 3: Field Testing (Smart Cart, Autonomous Retail Usability)
Field Testing
description: For the final project, we tested another team's concept for a 100L smart shopping cart. I co-designed a guerrilla usability test at a Leclerc supermarket in Pessac with 9 real shoppers.

To simulate the experience without a real digital cart, we used a Figma prototype paired with a physical cart token and a cardboard store map. Taking advantage of the unbuilt cart to evaluated spatial navigation efficiently.

sections.title: Findings
description: Every shopper managed to pair their app with the cart, but the concept itself had flaws. Five out of the nine shoppers instinctively tried to go to a physical cashier instead of using the digital checkout.

More importantly, people preferred their paper grocery lists and felt the app made them lose the initiative to think. Shoppers just didn't see the utility of the app, proving it was a complex solution to a problem that didn't exist.

sections.title: Impact and Reflections
description: Working across three different projects taught me a lot about focusing on what actually matters. On DeskFriend, taking the time to wireframe early saved us from over-designing. And with the Smart Cart, we learned the hard way that a polished UI doesn't matter if the product doesn't solve a real user need. Sometimes, realizing people just prefer paper is the most valuable insight you can get.

projects.title: Card sorting
projects.shortDescription: aligning tooling with student mental models
context: Problem: The Bordeaux INP student portal displayed 33 different tools in a single, unorganized grid. Finding the right service was frustrating because nothing was grouped by theme, forcing users to scan the entire page every time.

Outcome: We reorganized the portal into 12 intuitive categories based on how students naturally group them. We also renamed 7 confusing acronyms so users immediately understand what they are clicking on.

sections.title: Context
description: The university portal had 33 essential tools sitting in a flat grid. Because the layout was based on institutional habits rather than how students think, users had to scan the whole page just to find one tool.

sections.title: Our Approach
description: To fix this, I co-led an open card sorting study. We focused on a group of 9 students, since they are the primary daily users, to see how they naturally categorize these services.

sections.title: What We Found
description: Even with a small group, building a similarity matrix showed clear trends. For example, students almost always grouped their timetable (ADE) with the learning platform (Moodle). This led us to create a dedicated 'Essentiels' category for daily tools.

We also found that institutional acronyms and vendor names were confusing. I fixed this by renaming 7 items to describe what they actually do. For instance, we changed the vague 'Marsha' to 'Visioconférence - Marsha' and 'ODF' to 'Offre de Formation'.

sections.title: The Solution
description: We turned these findings into a Figma mockup. The new design organized the 33 tools into 12 clear, student-validated categories (like Administratif, Mobilité, and Assistance), with everything sorted alphabetically inside.

sections.title: Next Steps
description: During the study, some tools like 'Evacataires' were left completely isolated because they didn't make sense to students. Instead of forcing them into the layout, we recommended personalizing the portal based on roles. That way, students, teachers, and staff only see the tools relevant to them.

projects.title: Figma fundamentals
context: Summary: ENSC engineering students had to build UI prototypes for their projects but lacked formal Figma training, resulting in messy files and broken layouts. I created a comprehensive 94-slide Figma course covering everything from the basics to developer handoff, and gave it to the faculty to use as a teaching asset.

sections.title: The Challenge
description: At ENSC, engineering students have to build interactive UI prototypes for their projects. But without formal Figma training, most students just relied on trial and error. This led to messy files, broken layouts, and inconsistent interfaces, which made user testing and developer handoffs a lot harder than they needed to be.

sections.title: Building the Course
description: I wanted to help students replace guesswork with solid basics, so I built a 94-slide course directly inside Figma. To keep things clear and easy to follow, I skipped static screenshots and drew vector diagrams to explain concepts like Auto Layout, nesting, and variables.

I am also developing practical exercises based on the actual projects they have to deliver for school. These tutorials will walk them through things like making scalable buttons, setting up component variants, and using variables.

sections.title: Handing it Over
sections.description: After getting feedback from my classmates to make sure everything worked well, I gave the finished course to the ENSC faculty. I started this on my own to give professors who aren't Figma experts a ready-to-use resource for their classes.

sections.title: Impact
sections.description: By sharing this course with the school, the goal is to help future students build clean, testable prototypes that actually look and work like professional software.

context: Problem: I needed to teach the basics of UX design and Figma to 15 high school students during my internship at ENSC. Professional design tools can be overwhelming, so I had to create a 4-hour workshop that was simple, accessible, and hands-on.

Outcome: I built a custom tutorial website and ran a 2.5-hour design sprint where students designed a music app called 'Orchestra'. By the end of the session, all three groups successfully built and presented their own multi-page wireframes.

sections.title: The Challenge
description: During my internship, I had to introduce 15 high schoolers to UX design. Figma is a complex tool that can easily confuse beginners. My goal was to cut out the jargon and design a 4-hour workshop that felt approachable and genuinely fun to complete.

sections.title: Teaching the Basics
description: I started with a 30-minute presentation directly inside Figma to show them how frames, layers, and typography work. To help them practice, I coded a simple website hosting step-by-step video tutorials. Before the actual day, I timed this tutorial with someone who had little experience with Figma to make sure the pacing was realistic for our 4-hour window.

sections.title: The Design Sprint
description: The main event was a 2.5-hour hands-on session where the students split into three groups to design a desktop music streaming app named 'Orchestra'. I acted as the client and gave them specific guidelines to follow. To get them thinking about accessibility, I also asked them to include a dedicated 'Handi-sons' section in their app.

sections.title: How It Went
description: Keeping a group of teenagers focused for four hours is definitely a challenge. But every team managed to build a working multi-page wireframe. I walked around the room helping them fix basic issues with layers and alignment. We wrapped up with the students presenting their design choices, proving that beginners can pick up UX concepts quickly when you give them the right support.

playgrounds.title: kfé
playgrounds.shortDescription: redesign of a coffee shop's mobile app
context: Problem: I had a one-week sprint to design a mobile beverage ordering app for a demanding client who gave minimal initial specifications. The challenge was extracting their hidden business rules and turning them into a functional, user-friendly product.

Outcome: I initially built a functional prototype based on strict client rules. Later, I redesigned the app with warmer colors, a flexible Figma component system, and a streamlined menu that lets users customize drinks without leaving the main screen.

sections.title: Getting Clarity
description: I had a tight deadline and very vague instructions, so I led the discovery phase to figure out exactly how the app needed to work.

sections.title: Agile Discovery
description: By asking the right questions, I uncovered a few strict rules: the app had to use the brand's corporate green, stick to three specific sizes, and only allow milk and sugar as add-ons. Knowing this helped me plan the data structure to calculate cart totals and pricing before I even started designing.

sections.title: Simplifying the Menu
description: I wanted to make the app as frictionless as possible. Instead of sending users through multiple screens to customize a drink, I added expanding cards right on the main menu during the redesign. Now, people can pick their size, milk, and sweetness using simple buttons and sliders without losing their place in the list.

I also changed the visual style. The original corporate green didn't feel like a food app, so I swapped it for warm oranges and coffee browns. This makes the interface feel much more appetizing and inviting.

sections.title: Adaptive Checkout
description: The checkout flow changes based on what the user needs. If they want delivery, they have to enter a valid address before the payment button becomes active. If they choose pickup, the app finds the nearest store and immediately shows quick payment options like Apple Pay.

sections.title: Cart & Order Tracking
description: To help increase the average order value, I added a 'Want a snack with that?' prompt right in the cart. I also wanted to keep users from worrying after they pay. The app shows a continuous status bar and a three-step visual timeline so they always know exactly when their coffee will be ready.

sections.title: Scalable Component System
description: To make all of this work, I built a clean UI kit in Figma. Instead of making dozens of static screens, I used variants and boolean properties. This kept the component library small but flexible enough to handle all the different drink sizes, add-ons, and cart states.

playgrounds.title: mates
playgrounds.shortDescription: comprehensive brand ecosystem and print assets
context: Problem: The founders of Mates, a student note-sharing platform, needed a brand identity that highlighted community and trust without feeling like a boring academic tool. They came with specific constraints, including a wolf motif, the Inter font, and a blue and orange color palette.

Outcome: I designed a complete brand system centered around a custom wolf logo and a highly readable digital color palette. I handed everything off in an organized Figma library, giving the founders the assets they needed to launch the brand on their own.

sections.title: The Challenge
description: The founders of Mates wanted their peer-to-peer note-sharing platform to feel supportive and dynamic. They gave me a strict list of visual rules to follow:

• integrate the letter M
• use a wolf or ant motif
• stick to the Inter typeface
• use a blue and orange color palette

sections.title: The Design Process
description: To meet their requirements, I designed a logo that naturally blends the letter M into the silhouette of a howling wolf. I used basic grids and clear spacing to make sure the icon looked balanced whether it was a tiny digital badge or printed on a large banner.

While testing the requested blue and orange palette, I realized the colors would cause contrast and readability issues on digital screens. I showed the founders a few side-by-side alternatives in Figma. Seeing the options helped them agree to drop the orange and switch to a cleaner, high-contrast mix of Byzantine Blue (#194DDF), Eerie Black (#212121), and White Smoke (#F3F3F3).

sections.title: Brand Assets
description: Beyond the main logo, I put together the rest of their digital and physical assets. This included social media templates for platforms like LinkedIn, TikTok, and Instagram, along with custom illustrations and a repeating background pattern made from the wolf shape. For their campus marketing, I designed A5 flyers with a QR code and enough blank space at the bottom to meet standard legal print requirements.

sections.title: The Handoff
description: When the work was done, I organized all the assets and templates into a clean Figma library. I handed the files over to the founders so they could immediately start using the brand system and creating their own content without needing me to build every new post.

playgrounds.title: krystal
playgrounds.shortDescription: elements visual identity for sports events
context: Problem: Krystal, a sports tournament for eight engineering schools, needed a complete set of themed T-shirt designs delivered in just two weeks. The designs had to work as single-color screen prints on eight different shirt colors.

Outcome: I created a modular logo system based on a diamond shape, which saved time and kept the branding consistent across all the schools. By getting approval on paper sketches first, I was able to hand off the final print-ready files without needing any revisions.

sections.title: The Challenge
description: Krystal is an annual sports tournament for the Bordeaux INP network that brings together over 500 students from eight engineering schools. They asked me to design the event's clothing around an 'Elemental Forces' theme. The main constraint was the timeline: I only had two weeks to deliver all the final files. Additionally, the designs had to be single-color screen prints that would look good on several different T-shirt colors.

sections.title: The Design System
description: With such a tight deadline, I decided to build a simple modular system using a split diamond shape. I kept the bottom half of the diamond exactly the same across all designs to tie the eight schools together, and customized the top half for each school's assigned element. This approach kept the chest badges clean and recognizable, and it let me treat the graphics almost like a reusable component library.

sections.title: Sketching First
description: Because I didn't have time to endlessly tweak vectors on a screen, I did all the initial brainstorming on paper. This kept the process fast and natural. Simpler themes like Fire and Water were easy to nail down, while trickier ones like Time and Spirit took a few pages of iteration to get right. Getting the organizers to agree on the pencil sketches first meant that by the time I opened my design software, I knew exactly what I was building.

sections.title: Designing for Print
description: Screen printing has strict limits. To make sure the logos popped on the eight different shirt colors, I set up the vectors using careful line weights and negative space to give the flat shapes a bit of 3D volume.

sections.title: The Handoff
description: I delivered every logo in both light and dark versions. Because the files were set up cleanly from the start, the garment vendors were able to print everything flawlessly on the first try without coming back to me for any fixes.

playgrounds.title: krystal
playgrounds.shortDescription: elements visual identity for sports events
context: Problem: Krystal is a sports tournament for over 500 students across eight engineering schools. I needed to design T-shirts that unified the schools under one main brand, while adapting to a specific movie theme assigned to each team.

Outcome: I designed a core sports crest and created eight custom variations based on films like Avatar and Minions.I delivered all the final designs as print-ready, single-color vectors optimized for eight different T-shirt colors.

sections.title: The Challenge
description: Krystal is a two-day sports tournament for eight engineering schools in the Bordeaux INP network. For the 2025 edition, the organizers gave each participating school a distinct movie theme. I was brought in to design the T-shirt graphics for all eight teams. The challenge was to make each shirt fit its assigned movie while making sure they all clearly looked like part of the same tournament.

sections.title: The Design System
description: To tie everything together, I designed a main sports crest. It included a central diamond shape, a trophy, laurel wreaths, a crown, and hand-drawn lettering for the tournament name. This gave the event a consistent athletic look.

Once I had this base design, I customized the central diamond for each school's theme. For example, I added a skull and swords for Pirates of the Caribbean, Na'vi markings for Avatar, a surfboard for Brice de Nice, goggles for Minions,french fries for Les Tuches, a tie for Baby Boss, a dinosaur skull for RRRrrrr!!!, and a cowboy hat for The Good, the Bad and the Ugly.

sections.title: Designing for Print
description: The T-shirts needed a small logo on the front and a large one on the back. I kept the front chest badge simple and bold so it was easy to read from a distance during games. For the back, I used the full, detailed crest.

The printer required single-color vectors. Since every school had a different colored shirt (like red, green, purple, or yellow), I prepared light and dark versions of every design to make sure the ink would have enough contrast against the fabric.

sections.title: Takeaways
description: Over the two months, I shared multiple iterations with the organizing committee to make sure we were aligned on each movie theme. Balancing a unified tournament brand with eight playful, separate themes was a great exercise in working within constraints. In the end, I delivered a print-ready package that gave all 500 participants a unique team shirt while keeping the overall event identity clear.
